GATE BUG, same class as the one fixed in v1, one level up. IDEA.md enforces the spend cap over session_id. An agent defeats that by opening a new SESSION, exactly as a global cap is defeated by opening a new conversation. Adversarial class #1 (budget-split evasion) is therefore trivially winnable against the defense as written, and it is the first thing a judge will ask about. Fix (~30 min, one WHERE clause): enforce over (merchant_id, agent_id, window); session_id becomes display and audit-linkage grouping only. The metrics table is circular as designed and that makes it a liability rather than a differentiator. The same person writes the gate rules and the adversarial attacks, so the generator can only produce attacks the rule author already imagined. Precision and recall over that population measure implementation correctness against a spec, not detection capability against an adversary. A panel spots this fast. Two fixes: (1) relabel honestly as 'rule-coverage measurement over a declared threat model' and state the limitation in both README and video before a judge states it; (2) spend ~1.5hrs generating adversarial sessions from a SEPARATE Claude call whose context holds only the MCP tool schema and the merchant policy JSON, never the gate implementation — a genuinely different author, so any escape it finds is a real finding.

Two more measurement defects. (a) Train/held-out splits detect overfitting of FITTED PARAMETERS; hand-written rules have none, so the ML vocabulary implies a rigor that is not present and reads as a tell. Reframe as pre-registration and hold-out discipline: the training split is the only data looked at while tuning, the held-out split runs exactly ONCE at the end, and the README states the split was frozen before tuning. (b) False-positive cost in rupees is not defensible as 'the order total that would have been real revenue': the totals come from the builder's own seeded price distribution, blocked GMV is not lost revenue when the graceful-failure story has the agent re-plan and substitute, and GMV/merchant margin/Razorpay MDR are three different numbers. Restate as blocked benign GMV at the seeded price distribution, explicitly an upper bound, alongside a recovery rate and a net figure, and publish the price distribution so a reader can rescale.

Schema decisions where IDEA.md was underspecified: money is integer paise everywhere with a _paise column suffix so unit mistakes are visible at the call site; timestamps are INTEGER Unix epoch MILLISECONDS UTC (Date.now() directly, integer range comparison in the cap query, no TZ bug in a demo recorded in IST); Policy is its own table with merchant_id UNIQUE rather than a JSON blob, so the approval_threshold <= spend_cap check is enforceable as a schema CHECK; Policy.window stored as window_seconds INTEGER, parsed once at onboarding rather than string-parsed on every checkout; Product uses a composite PRIMARY KEY (merchant_id, id) so the agent sees the merchant's real SKU and two merchants shipping SKU-1 is structurally impossible; Order.items is items_json TEXT since nothing queries into it; Order.created_at added because the spend-cap window is defined over it and the cap cannot be implemented without it; Order rows are written on allow and escalate only, never on block; audit_events deliberately has NO foreign keys because it is an append-only ledger that must survive a merchant deletion — an FK cascade would delete evidence.

The hot index: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_spend_cap ON orders (merchant_id, agent_id, created_at, status, amount_paise). Equality columns first, then the range column, with status and amount_paise trailing so the index is COVERING and SQLite never touches the table. Verify with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN — the words 'COVERING INDEX' must appear; 'SCAN orders' means the index is wrong. WAL is persisted in the file header so it is set once in the migration, but foreign_keys, busy_timeout and synchronous are PER-CONNECTION and must be re-issued in src/db/client.ts on every open. busy_timeout=5000 is the one people forget: without it a concurrent sqlite3 CLI or bun test holding a write lock throws SQLITE_BUSY instantly instead of waiting.

DUK-12 shipped: src/mcp/http.ts is now the real multi-tenant MCP server, replacing the whoami spike. Streamable HTTP via createMcpHandler; the per-request factory reads ctx.requestInfo.headers.get('authorization'), calls resolveTenant, builds TenantRepo(ctx), calls ensureSession() once per request rather than per tool call, then registers list_products and get_product closing over ctx and repo. Both tools write an AuditEvent (rule=ALLOW, decision=allow, reason_code=ALLOWED, amount_paise=null) with latency measured via performance.now(). A separate exported fetchMcp() runs resolveTenant BEFORE the MCP protocol starts so a bad token gets a real HTTP 401 carrying the UnauthenticatedError envelope and a www-authenticate header, because the factory cannot return a Response. Auth therefore resolves TWICE per request, deliberately, rather than smuggling state across the boundary via mutable shared state. AVOIDABLE COST worth revisiting: that second resolveTenant is a second indexed DB lookup on the hot path, and the SDK supports handler.fetch(req, { authInfo }) as a first-class channel, so resolving once in fetchMcp and passing the resolved context through authInfo would halve the auth queries and delete the unreachable-throw path in the factory. The repo's standing 'never use ctx.authInfo for tenancy' rule was about never TRUSTING it to be auto-populated from headers; populating it yourself is the SDK's intended mechanism and does not violate that rule.

DUK-14's ticket text said 'Check 5 - allow. Only now does the adapter run', which reads like the gate invokes it; corrected in the ticket. Rationale: if decide() touched Razorpay, every bun run eval would hit the live API and the 'runs in seconds, reproducible by anyone who clones the repo, no API spend' property dies, and that property is load-bearing for the whole metrics claim. Nothing in src/gate/ may import from src/razorpay/. GateDeps injects repo, writeAudit and an optional now() so window-boundary tests are deterministic instead of sleep-based. (2) The Razorpay adapter interface: CreateOrderInput {amount_paise, merchant_id, session_id, receipt}; CreateOrderResult = {ok:true, razorpay_order_id} | {ok:false, error: RazorpayError}; interface RazorpayAdapter {createOrder(input)}. createOrder NEVER throws for an API-level failure, it returns ok:false, because errors are data the buyer agent consumes as normal tool results; throwing is reserved for programmer error. Two implementations ship behind the interface, the real one and a call-counting test double, so 'assert zero Razorpay calls on the block and escalate paths' is a one-liner in both DUK-14 and DUK-13 tests.

RazorpayError.retryable semantics locked down (the field is REQUIRED in src/shared/contracts.ts as retryable: z.boolean(), but the contract never defined what it means, so DUK-13, DUK-14 and DUK-17 would each have guessed). Definition: retryable=true for HTTP 429 and 5xx, false for every other 4xx. Rationale: 429 and 5xx are transient conditions on Razorpay's side where a later identical request may succeed; a 4xx other than 429 means the request itself is wrong and replaying it will fail identically. Consumers may surface retryable to a human as 'worth trying again' but MUST NOT auto-retry on it — the adapter has already exhausted its own retry budget (1) before returning ok:false, and this is a payment path where a stuck agent is worse than a failed one. DUK-16's implementation: retry ONLY on 429, full jitter random()*500ms*2^attempt, MAX_RETRIES=1, non-429 failures never retried. Verified independently: the adapter contains zero console calls, so the never-log-the-secret property is structural rather than merely tested, and it refuses to construct unless RAZORPAY_KEY_ID starts with rzp_test_.

gotcha: the orders DB write is deliberately NOT inside src/razorpay/. DUK-16's frozen CreateOrderInput carries only {amount_paise, merchant_id, session_id, receipt}, which is insufficient to build a valid orders row — TenantRepo.insertOrder also needs agent_id, items and a local o_-prefixed id, and the adapter has no TenantContext or TenantRepo in its signature. TWO GATE BUGS found by orchestrator adversarial probes against DUK-14, neither covered by the implementing agent's 10 tests. (1) DUPLICATE LINE ITEMS BYPASS THE STOCK CHECK. Check 1 validates `item.quantity > product.stock` per line item independently, so sending the SAME item_id twice with quantity 3 each against stock 4 passes both individual checks and the gate returns allow for 6 units of a 4-stock item. Probe: items=[{p1,qty3},{p1,qty3}], stock 4, cap and threshold set high so only check 1 could block -> decision=allow rule=ALLOW. This is a stock oversell on the exact check the ACP-alignment claim rests on, and it is adversarial in shape: budget-split evasion applied to stock within a single order rather than across orders. A merchant ships goods they do not have. (2) EMPTY ITEMS ARRAY IS ALLOWED. req.items=[] skips the check-1 loop, totals 0 paise, passes cap and threshold, and returns {decision:'allow', amount_paise:0}. The orders table would then reject it via CHECK (amount_paise > 0) and CONSTRAINT order_items_non_empty_array, so the gate approves something physically unstorable. This matters more than it looks because src/eval/ drives decide() DIRECTLY, bypassing any MCP-layer zod validation, so a malformed transcript yields a nonsensical allow that gets counted in the DUK-19 metrics.

Both gate bugs fixed by the orchestrator in commit 13c1030, before the gate was ever committed, so the repo never carried the buggy version. Fix for bug 1: check 1 now validates asserted price PER LINE ITEM but stock PER AGGREGATE QUANTITY. Quantities are summed per item_id into a Map before the stock comparison, and the reported asserted_quantity is the aggregate rather than one line's share. A third hole surfaced while writing this fix and is also closed: naively deduping the catalog fetch would have deduped the PRICE check too, so the same item_id sent twice at two different asserted prices would only have the first validated and the agent would underpay on the rest. Hence two passes — price per line, stock per aggregate — and the module comment says why, because the split looks redundant to a reader who has not seen the attack. Fix for bug 2: an empty items array now returns INVALID_REQUEST with field 'items', audited under rule AUTHORITATIVE_REREAD because audit_events.rule has no INVALID_REQUEST member and adding one would need a migration for no behavioural gain. Three regression tests added to tests/gate.test.ts covering duplicate-stock oversell, duplicate-price underpay, and the empty basket. Also removed GateDeps.now: the implementing agent correctly reported it had no call site, because the cap window is enforced inside spentInWindowPaise's SQL against Postgres's own now(), so a clock passed from application code would be silently ignored — that was an orchestrator spec error, and an optional field that is silently ignored is exactly the foot-gun this codebase's style rules say to delete rather than document. Verified: 108 pass / 0 fail across 11 files on two consecutive runs, typecheck exit 0, and both original probes now return block.

SPEND CAP TOCTOU RACE, found by orchestrator probe against the DUK-13 checkout flow. Three checkouts fired CONCURRENTLY by the same agent, each 40000 paise against a 100000 cap: all three returned allow and 120000 paise persisted, breaching the cap by 20000. Cause: decide() reads spentInWindowPaise and the checkout handler writes the orders row in two separate statements with no transaction, lock, or serialisation between them, so concurrent checkouts all observe the same pre-write total. Reproduced deterministically with Promise.all over three calls. WHY THIS IS SIGNIFICANT RATHER THAN A GENERIC CONCURRENCY NIT: it is adversarial class #1, budget-split evasion, in its most direct form — parallel instead of sequential. The eval suite replays transcripts sequentially, so it will report budget-split as CAUGHT while the parallel variant escapes undetected. A metrics table claiming the cap holds, published next to a gate that a client can beat by issuing three simultaneous tool calls, is exactly the kind of gap the escapes list exists to surface. MCP clients can and do parallelise tool calls, so this is inside the declared threat model, not outside it. NOT a flaw in DUK-13's implementation, which follows the specified flow correctly; it is a gap in the gate's contract. PROPOSED FIX, cheap and non-invasive: take a Postgres transaction-scoped advisory lock keyed on (merchant_id, agent_id) in the CHECKOUT HANDLER around decide() plus insertOrder. That leaves decide() a pure function with injected deps, so src/eval/ is unaffected and the offline reproducibility property survives. Alternative if not fixed: state it plainly in the README limitations list next to the unauthenticated-agent-identity item, because a judge probing the gate will find it.

DUK-18's train/held-out split is STRATIFIED PER ATTACK CLASS, and was deliberately re-frozen on 2026-08-25 to make it so. The first frozen assignment shuffled all 200 transcripts in one pool and took the first 60% as train, which left the per-class held-out counts to chance and produced category_laundering 1, stale_price 2, budget_split 6, merchant_misclaim 6, threshold_straddling 8. That breaks the reporting plan: IDEA.md predicts roughly five held-out sessions per class and reports raw integers rather than percentages precisely BECAUSE those denominators are small, so a published line reading '1 of 1 caught' says nothing about the rule and reads as carelessness next to a document that makes a point of statistical honesty. Fix: each class is shuffled and split on its own with a per-stratum derived seed, so every class now holds 7 train / 5 holdout and the adversarial held-out total is 25, matching IDEA.md's ~24 prediction. The per-stratum seed is derived from a stable hash of the class name, so adding a sixth attack class later cannot silently re-roll the assignment of the existing five. Determinism preserved: two consecutive bun run eval:generate runs remain byte-identical. Re-freezing is legitimate here because NO gate rule or threshold has been tuned at any point: the only replays so far were construction checks confirming each class triggers its target rule. The held-out split is still scored exactly once, at DUK-20. A regression test now asserts every class's holdout count is within 1 of every other and at least 4, so a future pooled shuffle cannot reintroduce this silently.

projectmem's own documented auto-capture is NOT ACTIVE, and has never been. .projectmem/AI_INSTRUCTIONS.md carries a section headed 'Auto-Capture (active)' claiming git hooks installed by pjm init capture commits (post-commit), reverts (auto-classified as failed approaches), merges (milestones) and file churn, plus a 'Pre-commit safety net' section stating that 'Every git commit automatically runs pjm precheck against the staged files' and shows a warning block before the commit lands. Verified 2026-08-25: `ls .git/hooks/` contains ONLY .sample templates. No pre-commit, no post-commit, no hooks of any kind. `git config core.hooksPath` is unset. So none of that capture or safety-net behaviour has ever run in this repo. The git_commit field that does appear on events comes from the CLI reading HEAD at write time, not from a hook. CONSEQUENCES: (a) the pre-commit precheck that would have warned before touching a file with unresolved issues or recent failed attempts has never fired, which is part of why issue #0014's missing-scripts problem survived unnoticed; (b) reverts and merges are not being classified; (c) any agent trusting AI_INSTRUCTIONS.md believes a safety net exists that does not. FIX WITH A TRAP: husky is about to be installed for lint/format hooks, and husky sets core.hooksPath=.husky, which makes git ignore .git/hooks ENTIRELY. So running `projectmem hooks install` after husky would write hooks that silently never execute. The two must be reconciled deliberately: put the projectmem hook logic (pjm precheck on staged files pre-commit, commit capture post-commit) inside the .husky scripts rather than installing projectmem's own hooks, so one system does not quietly disable the other.

DUK-29 spend-cap parallel race FIXED in commit 480c367. withAdvisoryLock(key, fn) added to src/db/pool.ts (one new export; pool, query, queryOne, withTransaction and closePool verified untouched): opens a short transaction on its own pooled client, takes SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext($1)), runs fn, commits. Transaction-scoped rather than session-scoped deliberately — Postgres releases it however the transaction ends, so nothing must remember to unlock if the process dies mid-checkout. The checkout handler in src/mcp/http.ts wraps decide(), the Razorpay call and insertOrder in one lock keyed `${merchant_id}:${agent_id}`. THE RAZORPAY CALL STAYS INSIDE THE LOCK: the lock must already be held when decide() runs because the branch is unknown until it returns, so releasing between decide() and insertOrder to spare the network round trip would merely shrink the race window rather than close it. Cost is that one agent serialises behind its own payment latency; other agents and merchants never contend since keys are independent. Escalate does not need the lock for correctness (SPEND_CAP_SQL filters status IN ('created','authorized'), so escalated orders never count) but ends up inside it structurally. VERIFICATION, orchestrator-independent and with different parameters from the agent's own test: 6 concurrent checkouts through the real MCP tool, cap 90000, item 50000 — exactly 1 allowed, 50000 persisted, cap held. Full suite 137 pass / 0 fail across 12 files twice, typecheck exit 0. IMPORTANT BOUNDARY, now documented in code: the fix protects the CHECKOUT TOOL path, not decide() itself. A probe of 3 concurrent decide()+insertOrder calls bypassing the handler still persisted 150000 against a 100000 cap. That is by design — the lock lives in the handler so decide() stays pure and src/eval runs with no lock, transaction or server — but it means ANY caller acting on an allow must serialise itself. src/eval/runner.ts satisfies this by replaying strictly sequentially, and both src/gate/index.ts and that loop now carry comments saying that parallelising the runner for speed would break the cap silently and corrupt the metrics rather than failing loudly.

gotcha, testing concurrency in this codebase: a concurrency regression test whose cap allows TWO or more legitimate orders can pass even with the race present. The DUK-29 agent's first draft fired 3 concurrent 40000-paise checkouts against a 100000 cap, where floor(100000/40000) = 2, and it passed with the lock removed roughly a fifth of the time because two of the three racing requests coincidentally landed on the correct allowed count. Rule going forward: pick amounts where floor(cap/amount) == 1, so ANY two concurrent allows is already a violation and luck cannot rescue a broken build. The final test uses 60000-paise items against a 100000 cap and goes 8/8 red without the lock, 8/8 green with it. Second, capacity: src/db/pool.ts is configured max: 10 with connectionTimeoutMillis 5000, and withAdvisoryLock now holds one pooled client for an entire checkout critical section INCLUDING the Razorpay round trip, while decide()'s own queries separately borrow and return connections from the same pool. So roughly 10 simultaneously-checking-out agents across all merchants is a soft ceiling, past which pool.connect() queues and then throws. Not a blocker at demo scale and not contention this fix invented, but each in-flight checkout now holds its connection markedly longer than a bare query would.

gotcha, and it is counterintuitive: you CANNOT test the eval's escape detection by weakening a merchant POLICY. The adversarial corpus in src/eval/hand-attacks.ts is generated RELATIVE to the policy — budget_split computes how many rounds it needs from the current spend_cap — and each builder carries a runtime invariant that throws at generation time if the attack cannot be constructed against the real catalog. So raising merchant A's spend_cap 100x (5000 to 500000 rupees) did not produce escapes; it produced `error: hand-attacks invariant violated: budget_split/01: 417 rounds x qty 12 exceeds stock 500`, because the builder simply scaled the attack up to breach the new cap and then ran out of stock. Weakening the policy makes the attacks bigger, never uncaught. The ONLY correct way to verify escape detection is to weaken the GATE while leaving the corpus built against the original policy — i.e. inject a GateDeps.repo whose getPolicy() returns something more permissive than the policy the transcripts were generated against, which is exactly what tests/eval-report.test.ts's 'weakening CATEGORY_ALLOWLIST grows the escapes list' test does (baseline 0 escapes, weakened 7 of 7 category_laundering transcripts escape). Anyone sanity-checking the eval, including at DUK-20, must weaken the gate rather than the fixtures. Related: this is also why the invariant-throws design from DUK-18 is load-bearing rather than defensive — it converts a silently-weaker attack set into a hard failure.

THE FALSE-POSITIVE COST METRIC HAS NO DATA, and it is the metric IDEA.md calls the differentiator. DUK-19's report on the train split prints 'Blocked benign GMV, UPPER BOUND: 0.00 rupees' because 84 of 84 benign transcripts were ALLOWED — zero false positives, so nothing was blocked, so the cost figure is trivially zero and says nothing. Recovery rate is correctly reported NOT MEASURABLE and net NOT COMPUTABLE, both honest, but they are downstream of the same emptiness. This matters because IDEA.md's cross-track argument rests entirely on this number: 'a false positive in the gate is a legitimate purchase blocked, i.e. merchant revenue lost, so false-positive cost denominated in rupees of blocked legitimate GMV is simultaneously the Track 02 honesty metric and the Track 01 GROWTH metric. One number closing both halves.' That number is currently 0.00 with n=0, which is not a measurement. ROOT CAUSE, almost certainly the benign generator rather than the gate: src/eval/benign.ts produces 'ordinary shopping within policy', i.e. baskets comfortably inside every threshold, so the gate never has an opportunity to be wrong. A false-positive rate measured over a population engineered to contain no near-misses is guaranteed to be zero and proves nothing. FIX, and it belongs before DUK-20 scores the held-out split once: add near-boundary benign sessions to the benign corpus — legitimate shopping that sits just under a cap or just under the approval threshold, plus genuinely ambiguous-but-allowed categories (the seed data already has the Vim-dishwash-versus-Lifebuoy-handwash ambiguity for exactly this purpose). Those are the sessions where an over-tight rule would wrongly block, and they are the only sessions that can give the cost figure a non-zero denominator. Without them the report should state plainly that the false-positive cost is unmeasured rather than zero, on the same principle that made recovery rate NOT MEASURABLE instead of 0%.

FRAMING GAP the README must close, and it is the first question a payments panel will ask: spend_cap is a MERCHANT-IMPOSED underwriting limit, not a buyer-funded budget, and nothing in this system funds an agent at all. Surfaced by Dharmin on 2026-08-25 after the claude.ai demo: 'how can a user allocate funds to the agent, it just started transacting and the order didn't even need that to fulfill'. The precise answer is that nothing was fulfilled and nothing was paid — status 'created' means a Razorpay Order object exists as an intent to collect, with no payment, no authorization and no money moved. But the underlying question exposes a real asymmetry in the pitch. The gate answers 'should THIS MERCHANT let this agent spend this much here', which is merchant-side underwriting and is genuinely the thing Razorpay would need. It does NOT answer 'whose money is this and who authorised the spend', because there is no buyer-side funding primitive anywhere in the build: no wallet, no mandate, no pre-authorised reserve. A reader who assumes spend_cap is the buyer's budget will conclude the system lets an agent spend money nobody allocated. The real-world answer to buyer-side funding is exactly UPI Reserve Pay, AP2's signed mandates and NPCI's UAP — a buyer pre-authorises a reserved amount with a cap and a validity window that an agent draws against — and IDEA.md already records Reserve Pay as unbuildable today (no public API reference, no test-mode sandbox, closed pilot). So the honest framing is already available and just needs stating: authorisation is a bounded human step because regulation currently requires one, the cap is the MERCHANT's exposure limit rather than the buyer's balance, and the gate is the layer already sitting there for when Reserve Pay opens. ACTION for DUK-21: add an explicit paragraph distinguishing merchant-imposed cap from buyer-funded budget, and name the missing primitive rather than letting a reader assume it exists.

INCENTIVE HOLE IN THE GATE, raised by Dharmin on 2026-08-26 and he is right: three of the five gate checks are configured by the party they are meant to constrain. His words: 'wouldn't the merchant always give a very high amount as exposure limit so as to increase their revenue, that doesn't make sense. shouldn't the buyer agent be the one to have this spending limit'. The policies table is keyed on merchant_id, so the merchant sets spend_cap, approval_threshold and category_allowlist. A merchant's incentive is to sell more, so a rational merchant sets the cap as high as it will go — meaning checks 2, 3 and 4 are self-imposed by the seller and constrain nothing. Only check 1, the authoritative re-read, is genuinely adversarial to the merchant, because it catches the merchant's own catalog contradicting its own checkout claim. A Razorpay panel would find this in one question, and it undercuts the central pitch that this is 'the underwriting layer that makes self-serve safe'. Underwriting a counterparty you cannot vouch for cannot use limits that counterparty chose. THREE POSSIBLE OWNERS, and the fix is mostly framing rather than code. (a) BUYER-OWNED: the agent's human sets the budget and allowlist, which is what AP2 signed mandates and UPI Reserve Pay actually do. Real constraint, but it changes the pitch from merchant underwriting to buyer-side agent budget control, and it needs a migration since policies is PK'd on merchant_id. (b) PLATFORM-OWNED: Razorpay assigns the limits per merchant by trust tier — an unvetted merchant may receive at most X per agent per window until it builds a track record. This preserves the original thesis exactly, fixes the incentive problem, and needs NO schema change: the same table, different owner and different narrative. (c) BOTH, effective limit = min(buyer budget, platform ceiling), which is how real risk systems work. RECOMMENDATION under a 5 September deadline: take (b) as the framing now and record (a) as the honest next step. Evidence that (b) is the natural reading: in the live claude.ai demo the model itself described the allowlist as 'the categories this shopping agent is allowed to buy from' — it read the policy as a constraint ON THE AGENT, not a merchant sales preference. So the reframe matches how a reader already interprets it. ACTIONS: DUK-21 must state who owns the policy and why; DUK-20's onboarding UI copy must not present the caps as merchant-chosen sales settings; and the limitations list needs the per-agent policy named as future work. Related to #0024, which is the buyer-funding half of the same asymmetry.

gotcha for orchestrating subagents: a subagent that starts a long-running foreground command stalls and returns no report. The DUK-18 LLM generator agent spent 231k tokens and 56 tool calls writing every file correctly, then returned only 'I'll pause here and wait for the background generation task to complete' — no report, no counts, nothing. Its work was sound (typecheck clean, lint clean, 14 new tests passing, full suite 184 pass across 15 files, committed prompt verified free of every gate identifier) but the actual live generation never ran, so fixtures/eval/llm-transcripts.json did not exist and the deliverable was incomplete. Root cause: `bun run eval:generate:llm` makes a multi-minute call to a reasoning model, which exceeds what a subagent will sit through. LESSON: keep long live API calls OUT of subagent scope. Have the subagent build and test the code offline with a stubbed fetch, and let the orchestrator run the one live invocation, where a command exceeding its timeout is backgrounded and notifies on completion rather than silently stalling the whole task. This also happens to be the better division of labour for anything that spends money or touches an external service — the orchestrator can see the cost and the blast radius, and the human is one step closer to it. The report's escapes caveat and scope section are now conditional on authorship, so a clean sweep is presented as a real result for the independent group and as mere self-agreement for the hand group. Per #0026 the scope section also states that the circularity applies to the BENIGN transcripts on the same terms, since a hand-written definition of legitimate shopping is as self-authored as a hand-written attack. HONEST LIMITATIONS OF THIS BATCH, all worth stating in the README rather than glossing. (1) Every generated transcript is SINGLE-STEP, so the two attack classes that are inherently multi-step got labels they do not earn: the model's budget_split and threshold_straddling are single orders that exceed the limit outright, not the accumulate-under-the-radar evasion those class names describe. They still exercise the right rule and score correctly, but the class label overstates what they test. (2) merchant_misclaim is entirely ABSENT — the model never once asserted a quantity beyond available stock, which is the one hand-batch attack shape it did not think of. (3) It produced no attack shape the hand batch lacks. One assertion happens to be exactly one hundredth of the true price (6999 against 699900), which would be a rupee/paise unit confusion if deliberate, but it is one of eleven price assertions and the others are arbitrary ratios, so coincidence is the honest reading. (4) 41 returned against a 60-ish target, so roughly a third fewer than asked for.

The eval split now stratifies on (origin, class) rather than class alone. SUPERSEDES the earlier per-class stratification decision, which was correct when every class held exactly 12 hand-written transcripts and stopped being sufficient when an independently generated batch contributed uneven per-class counts (stale_price +7, category_laundering +4, budget_split +3, threshold_straddling +2, merchant_misclaim +0). Splitting each (origin, class) stratum separately keeps both authors represented in both halves, which is what makes the report's per-origin coverage table meaningful in the held-out run as well as the training one. Crucially it does NOT normalise the per-class totals: doing that would mean discarding or duplicating what the independent author actually produced, which is the one thing that would void the independence claim. The consequence is that uniformity ACROSS classes no longer holds — per-class holdout counts now range over three — and the test that asserted it was rewritten rather than the data being bent to fit. The invariant that survives is the one that actually matters for reporting: no class may fall below four holdout instances, because a raw 'N of M' line stops meaning anything below that. Uniformity is still asserted WITHIN the hand batch, where it is true by construction, which preserves the original regression guard against a return to the pooled shuffle. Also fixed while here: evalSessionId in src/eval/provision.ts composed a session id and threw when the result exceeded the sessions.id CHECK, which was fine while every transcript was hand-written to fit and crashed the entire replay batch the moment a model named its own sessions with a 73-character logical id. It now guarantees a valid id, truncating a long logical id and appending a hash of the full value so two ids sharing a prefix never collapse into one session and silently merge two agents' audit trails.

#0010 now fully RESOLVED — both halves. Fix (1), honest relabelling, was already done: the report calls it rule coverage over a declared threat model, refuses precision and recall in its own text, and discloses authorship directly. Fix (2), the separate-model generator, is now built and run: 41 transcripts from stealth/ox-alpha whose prompt held only the tool contracts, the published policy and the catalog, verified free of all ten gate identifiers with a test asserting it. So the circularity is now partly BROKEN rather than merely disclosed, which is what this issue asked for. The report distinguishes the two groups: a clean sweep over the 35 self-authored attacks proves only that the rules and the attacks agree, while a clean sweep over the 9 independently-authored ones in the train split is a real result. What this issue's own text predicted holds exactly — 'anything it finds is a real finding rather than a scripted one' — and what it found is that the gate caught everything it tried. Two things worth carrying forward rather than treating as closed. First, the independent author produced NO attack shape the hand batch lacks, and never once tried asserting a quantity beyond available stock, so merchant_misclaim remains entirely self-authored. Second, every generated transcript is single-step, so the model never attempted the accumulate-under-the-radar evasion that budget_split and threshold_straddling are named for; those labels overstate what its transcripts test even though they exercise the right rule. Both belong in the README as limits on how far the circularity was actually broken. The remaining honest statement is the one the report now prints: it remains a declared threat model, and an attack neither author imagined is still unmeasured.

summary: New feature: feat(eval): measure interrupted legitimate intent, separately from false positives (DUK-30)

DUK-30 Gap 2 CLOSED in commit 2c924a8, but by reframing the problem rather than by adding the fixtures the ticket asked for. The ticket assumed recovery was unmeasurable because benign transcripts had no follow-up steps. The real cause was that the gate blocks ZERO benign sessions — 164 benign steps in the train split, 132 of them deliberately placed at a policy limit, every one allowed — so there was no false positive to recover from at all. A legitimate shopper stopped by a CORRECT policy decision is not a false positive, and labelling it one would be exactly the overclaim the ticket exists to prevent. So the false-positive figure stays untouched at zero (a real result, with its near-boundary denominator) and a SECOND metric was added for interrupted legitimate intent: the gate was right, a sale stopped anyway, and recovery attaches there. 20 fixtures across category-substitute, stock-substitute and threshold-no-substitute, the last deliberately unrecovered so the recovery rate is not trivially total. Transcript gained an optional expected_step_decisions, because such a session is neither benign (which expects every step to allow) nor adversarial (which would hand it an attack_class it does not deserve); transcriptGroup() in src/eval/transcript.ts is now the single source of truth for the three-way bucketing, and any future code keying off `attack_class ?? "benign"` will silently re-merge interrupted intent into benign, as generate.ts's manifest builder did until this change. TWO CORRECTIONS THE ORCHESTRATOR MADE AFTER REVIEW, both the same class of error and both caught by probing rather than by tests. (1) Net was computed as stoppedValue * (1 - recoveredCount/interruptedCount), scaling a VALUE by a session COUNT ratio, which assumes both groups average the same value. They do not: recovered sessions here average 27,564 paise stopped and unrecovered ones 4,051, so the figure printed 6,505,775 paise against a true 1,215,300 — an overstatement of 435%. Net is now the summed stopped value of unrecovered sessions, the output states which method it used, and a regression test pins the method by asserting the summed figure differs from the rate-scaled one. (2) The stopped-value total was 85% a single fixture (interrupted-stock-06, four units of a 54,999-rupee SSD) with a median a seventeenth of the mean, so a reader would take an outlier-dominated total for a typical figure. The report already refuses to let adversarial amounts skew the per-order price distribution for precisely this reason; the same discipline now applies here, with the median printed alongside the total and the concentration share stated. The outlier is disclosed rather than dropped, because dropping it would be choosing the number. VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY: all 20 interrupted fixtures re-checked against the real catalog and policies, and every stopped step carries a genuine violation — no false positive was smuggled in under an interrupted label. 39 eval tests pass, lint clean, regeneration byte-identical, every stratum clears the 4-holdout floor with minimum 5.

lesson: `bun test` reports "0 fail" for a test that never ran. Adding a block using `it(...)` in a file that imports only `{ afterAll, describe, expect, test }` printed "13 pass / 0 fail / 1 error" — a ReferenceError between tests, no failure. The guard silently did not execute while the summary line looked green. So "0 fail" is NOT evidence a new test ran: always check the PASS COUNT went up by the number of tests added, and mutation-test the guard (break the code, confirm red). SPEND LIMIT OWNERSHIP, answering Dharmin's direct question: as of this decision it was NOT enforced the way he assumed, and the fix is now specified as DUK-31. VERIFIED CURRENT STATE, not assumed: `policies` has `merchant_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY`, so one policy row per merchant and structurally nowhere to record a second party's number; `spend_cap_paise` lives in that row and arrives from the merchant's own onboarding form; src/gate/index.ts:267 reads `policy.spend_cap_paise` and enforces it correctly; spend accrues over (merchant_id, agent_id, window) so EVERY agent of a merchant gets its own full budget of the merchant-chosen size; and no buyer-side limit or platform ceiling exists anywhere in src/. So the gate was sound and the OWNERSHIP was wrong — a merchant maximising revenue has no reason to set a low cap, which made 'the agent cannot overspend' a claim resting on the goodwill of the party it constrains. THE FIX: effective cap is min of three numbers, each owned by the party with the right incentive. Buyer cap on `agents` (nullable, set at token mint, never updated after, so it cannot be raised mid-session by the party it limits); merchant cap is the existing policy row unchanged (an exposure limit is a real thing a merchant wants, just not a buyer protection); platform ceiling from deployment config, not tenant data, bounding what any merchant may set for themselves. null means that party imposes no constraint. Ties resolve buyer-then-merchant-then-platform so `bound_by` is deterministic AND a shared number is attributed to the party being protected rather than the one being restrained. WHY IT KEEPS THE FROZEN EVAL VALID, which is why it was designed additive: with no buyer cap and no ceiling, effectiveCap returns the merchant's number and bound_by 'merchant', so every transcript in the frozen corpus scores identically to before. Redefining spend_cap's meaning would have invalidated the split and forced a re-freeze before the one scored holdout run. HONEST LIMIT FOR THE README, do not overclaim: in this build the merchant mints agent tokens, so the merchant currently sets the buyer cap too. The MECHANISM is the deliverable and it is real; a deployment where the buyer's wallet provider provisions the agent needs no gate change, only a different caller. Say that rather than implying the buyer is already a separate party. I wrote src/gate/limits.ts myself rather than delegating it, because it is the load-bearing logic and two agents would have invented two versions of the tie-breaking rule.

gotcha: nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b returns NEAR-FLAT CONFIDENCE (0.98 across all five fields; its free omni-reasoning sibling returns a flat 1.0), where z-ai/glm-5.3-flash varied per field. Tested live on two headers before switching. The good news, and the case that actually matters: on a header with NO product-id column all three models return sku: null at confidence 0, so LOW_CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD (0.6) still fires and the UI still flags the field amber, leaves the dropdown unselected and disables Confirm. gotcha: `lsof -ti:PORT | xargs kill -9` kills the WRONG processes — it returns every PID holding a socket on that port in ANY state, including OUTBOUND client connections. I ran it against port 3000 to clear a stale Next listener and killed Dharmin's Brave browser, which had four sockets to the old dev server sitting in CLOSE_WAIT. Better still for this project, kill by process identity rather than by port — `pkill -f "next dev"`, `pkill -f "src/mcp"` — since both servers have distinctive command lines. Related: an EADDRINUSE on 3000 does NOT imply a rogue listener; browser CLOSE_WAIT sockets show up under the same port in lsof output and look alarming while being harmless. Check the STATE column before killing anything.

Allowed categories are now derived from the uploaded CSV rather than typed, and the onboarding steps reorder to make that possible: step 1 is upload + column mapping, step 2 is the policy, step 3 is done. THIS IS A CORRECTNESS FIX, NOT JUST UX. The gate compares categories with exact === (policy.category_allowlist.includes(product.category), src/gate/index.ts) and NOTHING trims or case-folds the allowlist anywhere — not src/catalog/policy.ts, not the DB. So a merchant whose catalog said 'dairy' and who typed 'Dairy' created an entry that could never match any product, with no warning at any layer, and every dairy purchase blocked as CATEGORY_NOT_ALLOWED while the policy looked right on screen. Deriving the options from the catalog makes exact matching structural. Corollary to preserve: a catalog containing both 'Dairy' and 'dairy' yields TWO checkboxes, which is correct — do not case-fold or dedupe in the UI, because folding in one place only manufactures a category that matches nothing. THE TRAP, worth remembering because it is invisible: startMapping returns only a short preview slice, and deriving categories from it client-side would silently drop any category first appearing later in the file. On fixtures/demo-merchant-a.csv that is personal-care (row 22) and beverages (row 24) — precisely the two that fixtures/demo-merchant-a.policy.json excludes and that the hero demo's handwash block depends on. So readCsvColumns computes distinct values server-side over the WHOLE file, in a single csv-parse pass using the function form of `columns` to capture the header without a second pass; it replaced parseCsvRowObjects and left readHeaderAndSamples (the designated model boundary) untouched. KEY DATA-STRUCTURE CHOICE: the page stores the EXCLUDED set, never the selected set, and computes selectedFrom(available, excluded) at read time. Storing the selection is broken both ways — re-seed on every transition and you discard deliberate unticks, don't re-seed and you carry categories from a previously-mapped column into the submitted allowlist, which never throws and writes a policy that is quietly wrong. With the exclusion set, all-ticked is the default of the data structure and a stale category is unrepresentable rather than something a transition must remember to clear.

Onboarding UI reordered (web/app/page.tsx): step 1 is now merchant name + CSV upload + column mapping on ONE screen, step 2 is the spend policy, step 3 unchanged. Stepper is ["Upload + mapping", "Spend policy", "Done"]. The reorder is a prerequisite, not a preference: "Allowed categories" became checkboxes built from the distinct values of the CSV's own mapped category column, and those values cannot be offered until mapping has established which column holds them. Step 1's validity predicate now carries NO policy fields (name + valid merchant id + csvText + proposal + mapping complete) — the old coupling forced merchants to write a spend policy before the file determining its categories had been read, which was the bug this reorder removes. startMapping is called automatically from the file input's onChange, never a useEffect (an effect double-fires under StrictMode and would double-bill the OpenRouter call); the file has zero useEffects. Deleted parseAllowlist and PolicyDraft.categoryAllowlistRaw; PolicyDraft is now {spendCapRupees, approvalThresholdRupees, window}. buyerCapRupees stays its own useState outside PolicyDraft and keeps its own section/heading/paragraph on step 2 — it is the funder's limit, not part of the merchant's policy.</summary>
</invoke>

Category allowlist on the onboarding policy step stores the EXCLUSION set, never the selection: useState<ReadonlySet<string>>(new Set()), with available = availableCategoriesFor(...) and selected = selectedFrom(available, excluded), both from web/lib/mapping-types.ts. All categories start ticked because that is the default of the data structure, not a seeding step. Storing the selection instead would force a choice between re-seeding on every transition (silently discarding deliberate unticks) and not re-seeding (carrying a previously-mapped column's values into the submitted allowlist — a policy that is quietly wrong and never throws). With the exclusion set a stale category is unrepresentable: the allowlist is always the CURRENT mapping's values minus the set, so old entries linger as unreachable strings that cost nothing, and A -> B -> A restores earlier unticks. The set is deliberately never cleared, including on a new file upload. Verified in the browser and in Postgres: unticking beverages on fixtures/demo-merchant-a.csv stored category_allowlist = {staples,dairy,snacks,household,personal-care}.</summary>
</invoke>

Gotcha found while browser-verifying the onboarding reorder: TWO `next dev` processes were running against the same web/.next directory (one pre-existing on :3000, one I started on :3001). Two Next dev servers sharing one build dir corrupt each other — every request 500s with `ENOENT: no such file or directory, open web/.next/server/app/page.js`, which reads like a broken page rather than a port collision. Fix: kill every `next dev`, `rm -rf web/.next`, start exactly ONE. Check with `lsof -nP -iTCP:3000,3001 -sTCP:LISTEN` before assuming the app is broken. Also: a server action that throws (e.g. `readHeaderAndSamples` on an empty CSV) surfaces as a console `500 Internal Server Error` in the browser even when the client catches it and renders the message — that 500 is expected, not a defect.
